memoryText: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Job 13:15 aloud, slowly, several times, and then try to say it from memory. Read the meditation and the review of the week, and then pick one of the three questions for writing, prayer, or conversation.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Job 13:15 is the sentence of a man who refuses two temptations at once.

The first temptation is to give up on God. Job has every reason to say that God is not good, that faith is a mistake, and that his friends were right about God being a tyrant. Instead he says, “I will hope in him.” The verb is the verb of waiting, of leaning, of staking everything on someone. And the “though” in front of it makes the hope costly. It does not wait for the circumstances to improve. It hopes while the worst is happening.

The second temptation is the opposite one: to pretend. The friends have told Job to be quiet and humble and accept his guilt. He refuses that too. “Yet I will argue my ways to his face.” He will not fake agreement. He is going to bring his case before God, in full honesty. His faith is not the silence of someone who has stopped asking. It is the courage of someone who believes that God can be asked.

Together, the two halves give you a picture of mature faith. It is not a calm faith that has no questions. It is a faith that has questions and takes them to God. Many of the saints have prayed this way. Learn it by heart, because you may need it in a hard season.

For the Christian, there is a final note. Jesus said something very close to this in the garden. He asked that the cup be taken from him, and he also said that the Father’s will be done. He hoped in the Father even though the Father would slay him, and the Father raised him up.
weekInReview: This week you read the middle of the book of Job. You heard Zophar tell Job that he cannot know the mind of God, and Job answer that he has no intention of giving up on God or on the truth. You read Job’s meditation on the shortness of life and his dim hope that a man who dies might live again. You read Psalm 22, the great cry of the forsaken and the song of the rescued, and you saw how Jesus prayed it from the cross. Then Bildad and Zophar piled on, and in the middle of the pain Job said, “I know that my Redeemer lives.” By the end of the week, Job was confronting the idea that the righteous always prosper, and longing to find God. The week taught that real faith asks, waits, and still holds on.
reflectionQuestions: Which is harder for you right now: to keep hoping in God when things go badly, or to bring him your honest questions? Write about what has made it difficult, and what one small step you could take.
How does Psalm 22, and the way Jesus prayed it, change the way you hear Job’s cry? What does it mean that the Redeemer Job longed for has been through the loneliest night himself?
Think of a person in your life who needs a faithful friend, someone who will not give easy answers. What could you do for them this week?
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you want to hope in him even though you do not understand.
Thank him for the Redeemer who walked the darkest night before you.
Rest in his care this Sabbath.
